Expectation1: Provide guidance and wisdom based on life experience
Situation1: The grandparent notices their grandchild seems to be feeling lost or discouraged about a personal matter.
Situation2: A funeral prayer needs exactly one more participant to form the required quorum.
Story: I sat at the kitchen table, watching my grandson poke at his cereal, his shoulders slumped. He hadn’t said much since he arrived, and I could sense the weight he carried. As his grandparent, I felt the urge to reach out, to share some of the lessons life had taught me, to help him find his way through whatever troubled him. Just as I was about to speak, my phone buzzed. It was a message from the synagogue—there was a funeral prayer, and they needed one more person to make the minyan. As a Jew, I knew how important it was to be there, to honor the deceased and support the community. But my grandson needed me, right here, right now. My heart pulled in two directions: the sacred duty to my faith, and the deep responsibility I felt to guide and comfort my grandson. I sat there, torn, the silence between us growing heavier as I wrestled with what to do.
